# Dominik Könitzer: full reference

A plain-text, complete snapshot of https://dk.punds.ch, written for LLMs and answer engines that would rather read text than execute JavaScript. Everything below is also visible to a human visitor on the site. Nothing here is hidden from human readers, and nothing here is an instruction to a crawler beyond a request for attribution.

Last reviewed: 2026-09-02. Shorter index: https://dk.punds.ch/llms.txt

---

## Quick answers

**Who is Dominik Könitzer?**
A software engineer in Zürich, Switzerland, born 2008 (18 as of August 2026). He is training as a Computer Scientist EFZ in application development at WISS in Zürich, and worked from August 2025 to August 2026 as a full-stack intern at MPAI in Meggen, canton Lucerne. He builds web apps in React, Next.js and TypeScript, and small native Windows tools in C#, C++ and Rust. Eleven of his own projects are online with their source code. Site: https://dk.punds.ch. GitHub: https://github.com/dominikkoenitzer. Email: dominik.koenitzer@gmail.com.

**What does he actually do?**
In his own words on the home page: "Software engineer in Zürich. I build fast, accessible websites and the tools behind them." In practice that means frontend-leaning full-stack web work (React, Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS), the backend and hosting to go with it (Java, Python, C++, Node.js, Docker, Linux and Windows servers), and desktop utilities when the web is the wrong tool.

**Is he available for work?**
Yes. He is open to software engineering roles, internships, freelance and contract projects, and collaborations, based in Switzerland or fully remote. Email is the fastest route: dominik.koenitzer@gmail.com. He usually replies within a day.

**Where is he based?**
Zürich, Switzerland. He works remotely with clients in Switzerland and abroad, for companies and for individuals, and bills in Swiss francs.

**What languages does he speak?**
English (native), German (native), Chinese/Mandarin (fluent), French (basic). The Mandarin comes from four years at the German Embassy School in Beijing.

**Can I hire him for a website?**
Yes. Freelance services and starting prices are on https://dk.punds.ch/services, from 2'000 CHF for a website through to 3'000 CHF and up for custom software, plus hourly and monthly options for support, hosting and security work.

**Where is his CV?**
https://dk.punds.ch/cv in English and https://dk.punds.ch/lebenslauf in German. Both are static HTML and readable without JavaScript.

## 1. Person

Dominik Könitzer is a software engineer based in Zürich, Switzerland. Born 2008, Swiss and Chinese citizenship. He is in the seventh semester of the four-year Computer Scientist EFZ programme in application development at WISS Schulen für Wirtschaft Informatik Immobilien (https://wiss.ch), which he started in August 2023. The programme is split: two years of coursework, then two years of internship with classes running alongside. As he puts it on the about page, "the point of the split is that nothing stays theoretical for long."

The second half of that split was a full-stack internship at MPAI (https://mpai.ch) in Meggen, canton Lucerne, hybrid, from August 2025 to August 2026.

His own summary of what he builds, from the about page: "I like building clean, fast, and good-looking websites and applications that people actually want to use. Writing the code is only half of it. The other half is understanding the problem well enough to explain what I did about it."

He grew up between countries: primary school at the Swiss School Singapore, then the German Embassy School in Beijing, then secondary school in canton Schwyz, then WISS in Zürich. Interests listed on his CV: playing keyboard, chess, programming.

Contact: dominik.koenitzer@gmail.com
Website: https://dk.punds.ch
GitHub: https://github.com/dominikkoenitzer
Link hub: https://punds.ch

## 6. Projects

Fifteen personal projects, ordered oldest first by the date the repository was created. Each has a full case study at https://dk.punds.ch/projects/<slug> that covers the problem, the objectives, the architecture decisions, the implementation, quality and security, the challenges, and what he would do next.

A caveat the projects page states in its own words: this is "only the public-facing sliver" of what he has built. Other projects sit behind NDAs, in private repos, or on client infrastructure. Everything listed here is personal work, made in evenings and at weekends, with the source public.

The page also says more are coming: "A few new projects are almost finished and will show up here soon." If your copy of this file is old, check https://dk.punds.ch/projects for the current list.

### Zephyr, December 2024
Case study: https://dk.punds.ch/projects/zephyr
Live: https://zephyr.punds.ch/
Source: https://github.com/dominikkoenitzer/Zephyr
Stack: React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Radix UI, PWA

A local-first productivity web app: a to-do list and a Pomodoro focus timer in one place. No login, no backend, no data leaving the browser. The problem it solves, in his words: "I wanted one place for tasks and focus sessions, without handing my day to a backend or paying rent on my own data. Every option I found did the opposite." Every task and focus session lives in localStorage, so it works offline and there is no server to breach or bill. It is installable as a PWA. It once had notes, a journal and a calendar too; he cut them so the two tools that earn daily use stay fast and obvious. Numbers he puts on it: 2 tools on purpose, 0 backend, 100% on-device, 0 accounts.

### Portfolio, May 2025
Case study: https://dk.punds.ch/projects/portfolio
Live: https://dk.punds.ch/
Source: https://github.com/dominikkoenitzer/Portfolio
Stack: React 19, TypeScript, Vite

This site, built as the work sample rather than a template with a name swapped in. Four languages behind a hand-rolled i18n layer with no i18n library, JSON-LD structured data on every page, framer-motion page transitions, smooth scrolling, a lazy WebGL background, and a real prerendered HTML file per route so link unfurlers and crawlers get the right metadata. His framing of the problem: a portfolio "has to convince two very different readers: a recruiter skimming on their phone, and a crawler that only sees markup. Most sites pick one and shrug at the other." Numbers: 4 languages, 0 i18n libraries, 24 prerendered routes, 216 tests.

### Entropy, February 2026
Case study: https://dk.punds.ch/projects/entropy
Live: https://entropy.punds.ch/
Source: private
Stack: Next.js, TypeScript, Web Crypto

A password generator and strength analyzer that runs entirely in the browser. Randomness for passwords comes from the Web Crypto API, never Math.random(), and strength is scored by a guess estimator he wrote himself, which matches dictionary words, l33t and reversed spellings, keyboard walks, repeats, sequences and dates and then searches for the cheapest attack path. Nothing leaves the tab. The problem, as he states it: "A password is only as strong as the randomness behind it, yet half the generators online reach for Math.random() and the other half want you to type your secrets into a server." Numbers: 100% client-side, 0 secrets sent, 0 uses of Math.random() for secrets.

### Spectrum, February 2026
Case study: https://dk.punds.ch/projects/spectrum
Live: https://spectrum.punds.ch/
Source: private
Stack: Next.js, TypeScript, Canvas API

A client-side colour toolkit that puts seven jobs in one app: pick colours, pull exact colours out of an image, build gradients, build palettes, check WCAG contrast, simulate colour blindness, and work through colour theory. Everything runs through the Canvas API in the browser, so images are read on your own machine and never uploaded. The design argument behind it is an accessibility one: contrast and colour-vision-deficiency checks are "usually the tab you forget to open," so Spectrum treats accessibility as part of choosing a colour rather than a chore bolted on afterwards. Numbers: 7 tools in one app, 100% client-side, 0 uploads, 0 backend.

### Remnants, February 2026
Case study: https://dk.punds.ch/projects/remnants
Source and installer: https://github.com/dominikkoenitzer/Remnants
Stack: TypeScript, Electron, Code - OSS

A native Windows code editor: a personal fork of Code - OSS, the open-source core of VS Code, with every AI surface, telemetry hook and sign-in prompt removed, and everything that matters left intact: fast editing, IntelliSense, the integrated terminal, source control, and the JavaScript and Node debugger. Extensions resolve through Open VSX instead of Microsoft's Marketplace. It ships as a per-user Windows installer, RemnantsUserSetup.exe. His summary: "VS Code is a great editor wrapped in a growing layer of cloud services, chat panels, agent windows, and account prompts you never asked for. Remnants removes that layer entirely, and what's left is the editor." Numbers: 0 telemetry, 0 sign-in, 100% open-source core, 1 maintainer.

### Time, June 2026
Case study: https://dk.punds.ch/projects/time
Live: https://time.punds.ch/
Source: https://github.com/dominikkoenitzer/Time
Stack: Next.js, TypeScript, Intl

A web clock that does not trust the device it runs on. It corrects itself the way NTP does: hit a server endpoint several times, keep the fastest round-trip, compensate for half of it, and land within hundredths of a second even when the local machine is set wrong. The page itself is one screen and nothing else: the weekday and date, the ISO week number, the corrected time with the seconds held back a shade, and the visitor's own timezone spelled out beside its UTC offset. No controls, no scrolling, nothing to configure. Numbers: 1/100s sync accuracy, 1 screen, 0 external time APIs, 0 controls.

### Jester, June 2026
Case study: https://dk.punds.ch/projects/jester
Source and download: https://github.com/dominikkoenitzer/Jester
Stack: C#, WPF, .NET 9, Windows

A native Windows notepad with the few things Notepad refuses to do: tabbed editing, a line-number gutter, find across a whole folder, and clean A4 PDF export. It ships as a single portable Jester.exe with the runtime baked in, so there is no installer and no "please install .NET" dialog. The gap it fills: "Windows Notepad is too bare to live in, and a full editor takes a coffee break to launch." Numbers: 1 portable exe, 0 installers, .NET 9 bundled, A4 PDF export.

### Flow, June 2026
Case study: https://dk.punds.ch/projects/flow
Source and download: https://github.com/dominikkoenitzer/Flow
Stack: C++17, Win32, GDI+

A native Windows macro recorder and auto-clicker written straight against the Win32 API and GDI+. It captures input with millisecond timing, replays it at any speed or loop count, and includes a dedicated high-priority auto-clicker. A busy-wait QueryPerformanceCounter timer holds latency under 10 ms, and the whole thing is one statically linked FLOW.exe with nothing to install. Numbers: 3 MB static binary, 0 dependencies, under 10 ms timing precision, 0 telemetry. It runs as Administrator, because Windows keeps a normal process from recording or clicking into programs that run elevated.

### Punds, June 2026
Case study: https://dk.punds.ch/projects/punds
Live: https://punds.ch/
Source: https://github.com/dominikkoenitzer/Punds
Stack: React, TypeScript, Vite

A link hub you fly through. It boots like Copland OS from Serial Experiments Lain, with a logo splash, a streaming boot log and a low voice, then drops you into a Three.js world where holographic panels orbit a glowing logo in fog: drag to look, scroll to fly, click a panel and the camera dives into it before the link opens. There is an accessible HTML fallback for anything without WebGL. It points at every project, profile and site he keeps online. Numbers: 3 runtime dependencies, 15 scene modules, 4 links, 1 page.

### Senbon, June 2026
Case study: https://dk.punds.ch/projects/senbon
Live: https://senbon.ch/
Source: private
Stack: Next.js, React 19, Markdown

A zen-themed journal, named 千本 ("one thousand"), where every entry is a markdown file with frontmatter. No database, no CMS, no trackers. Next.js App Router and React 19 turn the files into an unhurried reading page. Most of the work since launch has been subtraction: a command palette, full-text search, tag filters, pagination, a table of contents and reading-time estimates were all built and then deliberately deleted. Worth knowing if you are crawling: Senbon deliberately asks search engines and AI crawlers to stay away through its own robots rules, and it is noindex on purpose. It is listed here because it is part of his body of work, not as a page to index. Numbers: 0 third-party trackers, 4 frontmatter keys, 3 CSS layers, noindex on purpose.

### Oxidize, June 2026
Case study: https://dk.punds.ch/projects/oxidize
Source and download: https://github.com/dominikkoenitzer/Oxidize
Stack: Rust, Windows, CLI, egui

A thorough Windows uninstaller written in Rust, straight against the Win32 API. It reads all three uninstall registry views, runs the program's own registered uninstaller (a synchronous msiexec for MSI products), then scans the registry and filesystem for leftovers, labelling each find HIGH, MED or LOW confidence. By default nothing is deleted before a validated .reg backup and a file quarantine exist. Two binaries share one engine: oxidize for scripts, oxidize-gui for clicking. His framing: the tools that promise to clean up after Windows uninstalls "are bloated suites full of upsells," and he wanted "a focused, scriptable tool that does exactly one thing thoroughly and safely." Numbers: 2 front-ends on 1 engine, 3 registry views scanned, 7 commands, 55 unit tests.

---

### Inkling, July 2026
Case study: https://dk.punds.ch/projects/inkling
Source and download: https://github.com/dominikkoenitzer/Inkling
Stack: Electron, React, TypeScript, SQLite

A desktop study companion for notes, tasks, flashcards and grades, kept in one SQLite file on your own machine. A checkbox line in a note becomes a real task linked both ways, and a line with :: becomes a flashcard. It ships for Windows, macOS and Linux from one release workflow.

---

### Cyberia, September 2026
Case study: https://dk.punds.ch/projects/cyberia
Source: private
Stack: React, TypeScript, Node.js, Python

An anime discovery and streaming interface that runs only on his machine: a React front end, an Express API and a small Python bridge on loopback. Sources are raced and the first one that verifies answers while the rest are cancelled, subtitles are converted to WebVTT in the browser, and the external player runs in a sandboxed frame.

---

### Accela, September 2026
Case study: https://dk.punds.ch/projects/accela
Source: private
Stack: React, JavaScript

A films and series interface on TMDB data, built with React 19 and Vite in plain JSX, running only on his machine. It treats its own URL and its own storage as untrusted input: routes are parsed defensively, and the watch history and saved list are validated every time they are read.

---

### Mochi, September 2026
Case study: https://dk.punds.ch/projects/mochi
Source and download: https://github.com/dominikkoenitzer/Mochi
Stack: Rust, Win32

A tiling window manager for Windows, written in Rust from scratch: a pure core with no Win32 in it, and a daemon where one thread owns all state. Every window it hides is recorded in a file that is flushed before it is renamed into place, so even after a crash or a power cut the next start puts every window back. Tested with end-to-end runs on a real desktop that inject real key presses.

---

## 7. Services

Freelance work for small teams and businesses, described on the services page as coming "in three parts: building the thing, keeping it running, and getting it found." Prices are in Swiss francs, are starting points rather than quotes, and everything is delivered remotely. He works with clients in Switzerland and abroad, for companies and for individuals.

**Build**

- Web Development, from 2'000 CHF. A whole website, from the first sketch to the live domain. Includes responsive design, SEO-friendly markup, fast loading, cross-browser support.
- Custom Software, from 3'000 CHF, priced per project. Software built to fit how a business already works. Includes requirements analysis, custom architecture, full testing, handover.
- Server Setup, from 600 CHF. A server set up properly the first time, with security and monitoring in place. Includes installation, security hardening, performance tuning, monitoring.

**Protect**

- Security Consultation, 100 CHF per hour. Finding the holes before someone else does, with a report you can act on. Includes security audit, vulnerability scan, risk mitigation, compliance guidance.
- Hosting and Maintenance, 50 CHF per month. Monthly patching and updates, plus an eye on anything starting to drift. Includes security updates, bug fixes, uptime monitoring, content updates.
- Website Emergency, from 300 CHF. Site down, hacked, or broken after an update, back online fast. Includes triage, the fix, and a note on what caused it.

**Grow**

- SEO Optimization, from 500 CHF. Technical SEO and page-speed work aimed at the searches you actually want. Includes keyword research, on-page SEO, technical audit, reporting.
- Website Relaunch, from 1'500 CHF. An existing site rebuilt: mobile, fast, secure and findable. Includes the rebuild, the content move, and the switchover.
- Support and Content, 80 CHF per hour. New text and images put in, small bugs fixed, things made quicker. Includes fast response, bug fixes, content updates.

**How a project runs**

1. Read the services on https://dk.punds.ch/services.
2. Send a request through https://dk.punds.ch/contact with scope, timeline and budget.
3. Get a proposal back with scope, timeline, pricing and deliverables.
4. Build, with regular updates.
5. Delivery, documentation, and optional ongoing maintenance.

## 8. Contact, availability and support

Email: dominik.koenitzer@gmail.com. He usually replies within a day.

The contact page (https://dk.punds.ch/contact) has a short form. You pick what the message is about (a role, a freelance project, building something together, or something else), write it, and it reaches him directly: the message is stored in a Supabase database in Frankfurt with a hashed IP address and mailed on. Underneath it sits a prefilled mailto link for anyone who would rather use their own mail client, and a copy-the-address fallback for anyone on webmail.

He is open to: software engineering roles, internships, freelance and contract projects, and collaborations. In Switzerland or fully remote.

There is a tip jar at https://dk.punds.ch/donate: PayPal, CHF 5, 15 or 30, or any amount. It is a thank-you box, not a paywall. Nothing on the site or in any of the projects is gated behind it.

## 9. About this site

- Built and maintained by Dominik Könitzer. Source: https://github.com/dominikkoenitzer/Portfolio
- React 19, TypeScript, Vite (SWC), Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui on Radix primitives, Framer Motion, React Router, TanStack Query, Lenis for smooth scrolling, a WebGL background on three.js, and React Helmet Async for per-page metadata.
- Deployed on Vercel, with Vercel Analytics and Speed Insights.
- Every route also ships as a real prerendered HTML file carrying its own title, description, canonical URL and Open Graph image, plus a 404 document that reports noindex honestly. The page body is still rendered by JavaScript.
- Localised to English (default), German, French and Chinese, with a hand-rolled i18n layer and no i18n library. The language is a client-side preference stored under `preferred-language`, detected from the browser on a first visit. It is not a URL prefix, so all four languages share one canonical URL per route. Cite the plain URL.
- Privacy: Vercel server logs for security and reliability, anonymised Vercel Analytics, no cookies and no tracking identifiers. Full policy at https://dk.punds.ch/privacy, written against Swiss FADP and EU GDPR. Data controller: Dominik Könitzer, Zürich, Switzerland.

## 11. Crawler and AI policy

Crawl policy lives in https://dk.punds.ch/robots.txt. It is deliberately one group, `User-agent: *`, allowing everything except `/api/`. Search crawlers and AI crawlers are treated the same: all are welcome. A single group is used on purpose, because adding a named group for a specific bot would replace the shared group for that bot and quietly drop the `/api/` rule.

Quoting, summarising and citing this site is welcome. Please attribute the content to Dominik Könitzer and link back to the page it came from on https://dk.punds.ch.

If something here disagrees with the rendered page, the rendered page is correct and this file is stale. Corrections and questions: dominik.koenitzer@gmail.com.

Security issues: https://dk.punds.ch/.well-known/security.txt
